question: Move the AED at Edward A. Reynolds West Side High School into a 24/7 outdoor cabinet on the building's street wall.

evidence.text: Edward A. Reynolds West Side High School (School, ZIP 10029) has a registered AED at "11th Fl by cafeteria; FL 07; 9th Fl by Main Office".
Its hours come from: School building assumed open 7 AM to 6 PM on school days, September to June. Move the school-hours control to test other closing times.
Under that assumption it is reachable 55 of 168 hours in a school-year week, and 0 hours in a summer week if it is a school.
In 2025, an expected 1.18 cardiac-arrest 911 calls a year came from inside its two-minute walking area at hours when every AED in reach was shut (rank 10 of 100 NYC schools).
Within 400 m there are 10 other registered AED locations; 0 of them are open 24/7 by their published hours.
Citywide, a time-blind map puts 4.6% of call-weighted area within a two-minute walk of an AED; at the hour calls actually came in, 1.4% was within reach of one confirmed open.
Published research: a bystander shock with a public AED was associated with survival to discharge of 66.5% versus 43.0% without (Pollack et al., Circulation 2018, observed shockable public arrests).
Overture Maps lists no fire station, police station or hospital within 400 m.
Unknown to this data: cabinet cost, vandalism risk, whether the school already allows after-hours access, and the actual location of each 2025 call inside the ZIP (only ZIP-level data is public).

turns.speaker: advocate
turns.text: Moving this AED to a 24/7 outdoor cabinet addresses a real gap. The school's current location is unreachable 113 of 168 hours each week during the school year, and completely inaccessible in summer [E3]. Last year, 1.18 cardiac arrests occurred in the surrounding area when every nearby AED was closed [E4]. Research shows bystander shock with a public AED reaches 66.5% survival versus 43.0% without one [E7]. No fire station or hospital sits within walking distance [E8]. A street-wall cabinet would make this device available when it matters most.

turns.speaker: skeptic
turns.text: The proposal rests on incomplete data that obscures whether this specific move solves the problem. Yes, the current AED is inaccessible 113 hours weekly [E3], and 1.18 arrests occurred during closure hours [E4]—but we don't know where those calls actually happened within the ZIP code [E9], so we can't confirm a street-wall location would reach them. The survival benefit is real [E7], yet the 10 other nearby AEDs [E5] may already cover some gaps if repositioned instead. We lack cabinet cost, vandalism risk, and whether after-hours school access is already possible [E9]. Before moving this device, the council should map actual call locations and audit whether cheaper alternatives—like unlocking the school or relocating an existing AED—could close the same gap.

turns.speaker: advocate
turns.text: The skeptic is right that we lack the precise call locations within the ZIP [E9], and that's a genuine limitation. But the gap itself is undeniable: 1.18 arrests occurred when every nearby AED was shut [E4], and the 10 other registered devices in the area are also closed after hours [E5]. Even if we audited those locations, repositioning an existing AED still leaves the same core problem—no 24/7 access. A street-wall cabinet directly solves that, whereas unlocking the school building raises liability and operational questions the data doesn't address. The skeptic's call for mapping is sound, but shouldn't delay acting on the clear evidence of after-hours vulnerability.

turns.speaker: skeptic
turns.text: The advocate is right that repositioning existing AEDs wouldn't create 24/7 access if the underlying problem is that all 10 nearby devices close after hours [E5]. But that's precisely why we need the call-location data before committing to this specific site [E9]. The 1.18 arrests happened somewhere in the ZIP, possibly blocks away from the school's street wall—moving this AED there might not reach them at all. We also don't know cabinet cost or vandalism risk [E9], which could be substantial. A faster first step: ask the school whether after-hours access is already permitted, and map where those 1.18 calls actually occurred. That costs almost nothing and tells us whether this location solves the real problem or just feels like it does.

verdict.summary: Clear after-hours gap exists (1.18 arrests during closure [E4], 0 summer access [E3]), but precise call locations unknown [E9]. Investigate actual call sites and school access options before committing to cabinet installation.
verdict.strongestFor: 1.18 cardiac arrests occurred when all nearby AEDs closed [E4]; 66.5% survival with bystander shock [E7]; no hospital/fire station nearby [E8].
verdict.strongestAgainst: Unknown whether those 1.18 calls occurred at street-wall location [E9]; cabinet cost and vandalism risk unknown [E9]; cheaper alternatives (school access, existing AED relocation) not yet tested [E9].
verdict.nextStep: Map 2025 call locations within ZIP; confirm whether school permits after-hours access; estimate cabinet cost and vandalism risk before proceeding.
